newsitem.title: USA: De minimis changes unlikely in House - US Rep Archer.
newsitem.headline: De minimis changes unlikely in House - US Rep Archer.

text.p: U.S. House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer said Monday his panel's proposed scale-back of the so-called de minimis exemption for corporations is unlikely to change on the House floor.
"The bill that comes out of Ways and Means committee is going to be changed very little on the floor of the House," the Texas Republican said at a press briefing.

He said the bill, which Archer's panel approved on June 13, first goes to the House Rules Committee before hitting the floor at the end of this week. He said Rules is expected to make only "small changes" in the measure.
Archer added, however, that he cannot "prejudge" what may happen to de minimis and other provisions during a House-Senate conference on tax bills later this year.
"On the floor of the Senate there will probably be untold numbers of amendments," Archer said. "We have no way of knowing what the ultimate package will be...coming out of the Senate."
He added, "Therefore, I'm not going to try prejudge what the conference is going to have to adjust between the Senate bill and House bill until we see the final Senate bill."
Archer remarks came as PSA The Bond Market Trade Association showered House members with letters opposing de minimis repeal.
"We hope the final version of this year's tax legislation does not include" de minimis repeal, PSA Senior Vice President John Vogt said in the one-page letter.

Archer's panel voted June 13 to scale back the de minimis exemption for corporate holdings of munis to a flat $1 million, which muni lobbyists said would virtually gut the provision's usefulness for the muni market.
But the Senate Finance Committee cleared a tax bill on June 19 that includes no de minimis repeal provision.
Currently, the Internal Revenue Service does not permit businesses to deduct interest on debt that they use to finance the purchase of tax-exempt bonds.

But IRS said in 1972, in what is dubbed the de minimis rule, that it will not monitor whether a corporation has borrowed to purchase tax-exempt bonds as long as those holdings total less than two percent of a firm's net assets.
